segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Shoreside smelled of pine tar and sawdust, which is what a town smells like when it is growing out over water. Jory Brennick found the foreman of the stilt crew at the end of the unfinished walkway, where the planking stopped and there was nothing beyond it but the harbour. Selah Vance was a tall woman in an oiled coat, with a plumb line looped at her belt, and she was holding it out over the edge and watching where it hung.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Kettle Row. The short end, by the dyers. I'm told you're driving pilings there.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: Six days. The hammer frame comes round from the yard the day before and we set it on the morning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She drew the plumb line up hand over hand without looking at it.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: There's weather building out past the point. If it comes in early I start early, because I can't drive in a sea. That's not me being hard with you. That's the hammer.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: How early?

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: I'd not know until the morning it happened. Neither would you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud Brennick had already knelt and spread her chart on the dry planks, weighting one corner with a mallet she borrowed off a bollard without asking. The paper was soft at the folds from being rolled wet too many times.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: That's Kettle Row. There's the dyers' yard, and there's the shop with the apothecary's mark on the door lintel. Door faces the lane. Three steps down into the cellar and a hatch above them.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: Your chart's good?

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: My chart's honest. That's a different thing. I haven't been down that stretch since the tremor, and I'll tell you now the roofs moved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Selah looked at the chart for a while, the way people look at something they are not going to argue with.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: Then I'd go tomorrow, were I you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went in the grey part of the next morning, before the harbour traffic stirred the silt. Maud rowed. Jory went over the side first and Liora Quill a moment after him, and the water closed over them green and cold enough to make the chest tighten.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The lane was where the chart said. That much was true. The dyers' long vats were still bolted along the wall, furred with weed, and the lintel with the apothecary's mark on it stood at the right corner at the right height. Jory put his hand flat on the mark and felt the cut of it under the growth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Below the mark there were no three steps. There was a roof. The whole slate pitch of the house next door had come off its beams and slid into the lane, and it lay over the shop door at an angle, and everything beneath it was dark and tight and twenty years settled. Jory tried a corner with both hands. It did not move, and he had not expected it to.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They surfaced, breathed, and went down twice more, working along the fallen edge where the slate met the cellar wall. On the third dive Liora got Jory's wrist and pulled him round.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The tremor had pulled the wall apart four feet above the lane bed. The stones had slumped outward and left a gap a shoulder wide, open into black water, with weed drifting out of it in slow fingers. Jory came up with his hand still on the sill of it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Nobody's drawn that. Not on your chart, not on anyone's.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud leaned over the gunwale and looked at the flat water where he had come up, and she did not say anything for longer than Jory liked.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Then today it's the only door that shop has.
